title: Build spatiotemporal flowering maps
text:
Here is an example of combining the spatial prediction from deepbiosphere with the phenological prediction from the finite mixture models.














Comparing the finite mixture model distributions to the flowering records distribution, I can guess that the first distribution (dist = 1) corresponds with flowering.















Animation of growing degree days in PA





Use the matching finite mixture model curve for Cercis canadensis bloom reports to predict bloom probability from growing degree days

# use distribution 1
cc.d <- 1

cc.mu <- cc.mix$mu[cc.d]
cc.sigma <- cc.mix$sigma[cc.d]

pa_gdd <- rast("data-raw/big/pa_gdd2017_256m.tif")

# apply pnorm function to stack of gdd rasters
cc_gdd_cdf <- terra::app(pa_gdd, pnorm, mean = cc.mu, sd = cc.sigma)

# add a 0 raster at the beginning of the gdd time series to substract from
cc_gdd_0 <- pa_gdd[[1]]*0
cc_gdd_0cdf <- c(cc_gdd_0, cc_gdd_cdf)

# find difference in cumulative probability between weeks
cc_flrpb <- terra::diff(cc_gdd_0cdf, filename = "data-raw/big/flrpb_Ccanadensis.tif")




Animation of Cercis canadensis bloom probability in PA





Multiply species distribution from deepbiosphere with gdd-based bloom probability from finite mixture model to estimate overall probability of bloom occurence in space and time.

# load deepbiosphere raster
padf <- rast("data-raw/big/pa_2017_merge_block_mosaic.tif")

# Cercis canadensis
ccdf <- padf[["Cercis canadensis"]]

cc_stbp <- cc_flrpb * ccdf




Animation of C. canadensis spatiotemporal bloom occurence probability

title: Accuracy metrics for individual bee floral resources species
text: These are the individual accuracy metrics for bee floral resources species in each state.

title: Accuracy metrics for individual bee floral resources species
section: Accuracy metrics of floral resource species
text:
Accuracy metrics of floral resource species

Pennsylvania species








New York Species

title: Phenology
text:
Using rgbif, I searched for all research-grade iNaturalist observations of the top 100 floral resource plants across PA and NY within the NE US from 2016-2020. I matched these reports by location and week to growing degree day, estimated from 4-km PRISM data based on Sarah Goslee’s data and work. Data coverage is shown below.
Then I fit finite mixture models assuming normal distributions, using the mixtools R package. I tested fitting from 1 to 4 distributions and I’m showing the model with the lowest log-likelihood for each species in these results.
Data from GBIF includes occasional information on plant reproductive stage, if it was available from the observation. I’ve added this in these plots to provide some reference for the finite mixture model predictions, in orange.

title: Phenology
section: Top 50 reported flowering species phenology curves
text:
Top 50 reported flowering species phenology curves
Ordered by total number of observations, indicated in the upper right corner of each panel. Green histogram bars represent the distribution of the overall dataset, while orange bars represent just the records that explicitly report flowering. The curves are the finite mixture model estimates. Color of curves don’t mean anything except the order based on growing degree day.

text: Next 50 most reported flowering species

title: Accuracy metrics – spatial cross-validation
text: These are the results from conducting spatial cross validation. Because of the shapes of Pennsylvania and New York, I used 10 bands running North-South across these states as the test bands for 10-fold cross validation. Below I show the distributions for the overall model metrics for PA and NY. Significance comparisons are made between the cross-validation accuracy metrics of deepbiosphere and two conventional modeling approaches: Maxent trained on bioclimatic data and random forest trained on bioclimatic data.

title: Accuracy metrics – spatial cross-validation
text:
Binary classification metrics
These metrics threshold all probabilities ≥0.5 as present and <0.5 as absent for these metrics

Presence accuracy
The fraction of examples where the correct species observed at that location was predicted as present.



Comparing presence accuracy from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)




Precision score
Precision Measures how many species predicted to be present were actually present.



Comparing precision score from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)




Recall score
Recall Measures how many of the true species present are predicted as present.



Comparing recall score from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)




F1 score
F1 score The harmonic mean of precision and recall and represents a conservative mean of the two (i.e. is more affected by low values).



Comparing F1 score from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)

title: Accuracy metrics – spatial cross-validation
text:
Discrimination metrics
In order to take into account the effect of thresholds, discrimination metrics measure binary classification ability across a wide range of presence thresholds and describe the relationship between threshold change and performance change.

Area under curve [ROC] – uncalibrated
AUC ROC Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve averaged across species



Comparing ROC area under curve from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)




Area under curve [PRC] – uncalibrated
AUC PRC Average area under the precision-recall curve averaged across species



Comparing PRC area under curve from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)




Calibrated area under curves
A model which has extremely low predicted probabilities can still have a high AUCROC if within its range of predicted probabilities the model has good sensitivity and specificity for that class.

This means that it’s possible to have a model that never predicts a species as present with the standard presence/absence threshold of 0.5 yet still has a high average AUCROC.
To correct for this, Gillespie et al. (2024) also introduce a calibrated area under the curve score where the chosen thresholds are linearly interpolated values between 0 and 1.


Calibrated AUC [ROC]



Comparing calibrated ROC area under curve from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)




Calibrated AUC [PRC]



Comparing calibrated PRC area under curve from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)

title: Accuracy metrics – spatial cross-validation
text:
Ranking metrics
Top-K (top 1, 5, 30, 100) These metrics measure how many times the correct species was correctly predicted within the top-K highest-ranked species within a given image (where, for example, K=5 would be the 5 species with the highest probability of presence).

Species top 1



Comparing top 1 from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)




Species top 5



Comparing top 5 from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)




Species top 30



Comparing top 30 from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)

Comparing top 100 from spatial cross validation for Pennsylvania (left) and New York (right)

text: I experimented with thinning the species observations to retain only one entry per PRISM grid and week combination, in order to down-weight densely populated areas. Once again, I tested fitting from 1 to 4 distributions and I’m showing the model with the lowest log-likelihood for each species.

Metrics summaries
Below are the accuracy metrics reported by deepbiosphere along with explanations from the supplement of Gillespie et al. 2024. In the plots below I am showing the distributions of per-species metrics for the full species list and for bee floral resources. Significance comparisons are made between deepbiosphere and four other modeling approaches available in the deepbiosphere repository: BioclimMLP, a multilayer perceptron trained only on the Bioclim data; TResNet, a deep neural net model trained only on the NAIP imagery; Maxent, a maximum entropy modeling approach trained on bioclimatic data; and a random forest model trained on bioclimatic data.

title: Overview of deepflora project
text: A majority of crops and flowering plants rely on pollinators like bees, but bee populations are declining globally from habitat loss, pesticide exposure, and land cover change. Understanding habitat and floral resource availability is critically important for addressing these declines, and requires models of fine-scale floral dynamics across bee foraging landscapes and over growing seasons. However, comprehensive information is not available at the spatial and temporal resolutions relevant to bees, creating a gap that impedes understanding and conservation management.

title: Overview of deepflora project
text: A majority of crops and flowering plants rely on pollinators like bees, but bee populations are declining globally from habitat loss, pesticide exposure, and land cover change. Understanding habitat and floral resource availability is critically important for addressing these declines, and requires models of fine-scale floral dynamics across bee foraging landscapes and over growing seasons. However, comprehensive information is not available at the spatial and temporal resolutions relevant to bees, creating a gap that impedes understanding and conservation management.

title: Overview of deepflora project
text:
Methods

Spatial predictions
Using Deepbiosphere (Gillespie et al. 2024), we are modeling the joint distributions of bee floral resource plant species across Pennsylvania and New York, based on over 600,000 citizen science observations from iNaturalist, spanning 2012 to 2022. We use 1 m resolution NAIP aerial imagery from 2017 and 19 bioclimatic variables (BIOCLIM) to predict the spatial distributions of 100 bee floral resource species and over 2,000 other co-occurring plant species.



Deepbiosphere prediction for Cercis canadensis in Pennsylvania




Temporal predictions
To estimate bloom times, we are modeling the curves of seasonal peaks in citizen science observations (from iNaturalist) corresponding to flowering for the entire northeastern US, accounting for geographic variations in climate using thermal time (growing degree days).



Weekly growing degree day progression in Pennsylvania over 2017


We are applying a finite mixture modeling approach to approximate the distribution of bloom observations over growing degree day. Because we are using mostly unsorted citizen science data, all kinds of reproductive life stages are included in addition to blooming. By assuming that the overall distribution of iNaturalist reports for a species represents a mixture of multiple normal distributions, we can single out a curve that best fits the species’ bloom phenology.



Distribution of observation frequency for Cercis canadensis over growing degree days in 2017. Smaller orange distribution represents observations with annotations indicating that flowers were observed. In this case, distribution 1 matches blooming.




Combined spatial and temporal predictions
We can then combine the Deepbiosphere spatial distribution model with the finite mixture model-derived bloom curve over thermal time to estimate blooms over space and time.



Probability of bloom based on deepbiosphere and bloom prediction
